Pool Service in Mesa, AZ, Zone by Zone

Mesa splits its water service into zones, and the hardness of your tap water depends on which one you are in. Call the free line any hour to be put through to an independent, locally owned pool service company in Mesa.

Pool service in Mesa, AZ, comes down to two things the city publishes in plain sight: how hard the water is in your zone, and where pool water may go when it leaves the yard. Both shape how a Mesa pool should be cared for. Here is what they mean for your pool, and what the free line does.

Phoenix Pool Cleaning Pro does not clean or repair pools. When you call (623) 240-0428, an automated assistant gets a quick description of the pool problem, then hands the call to an independent, locally owned pool service company that works in Mesa. That company inspects, sets its own price and does the work, and you pay it, not the line.

Mesa: one city, several water zones

The City of Mesa serves drinking water from both surface water and groundwater wells, and its annual report explains that the wells themselves differ in how many minerals they carry. Instead of one citywide number, the 2025 report, issued in 2026, sorts hardness by zone. Homes in the City Zone average about 12 grains per gallon. Homes in the Eastern and Southern zones average about 16. Across the whole city, Mesa's water quality page puts the range at 12 to 22 grains per gallon, depending on which source reaches your tap.

To compare that with a pool test strip, multiply grains by 17.1 to get parts per million. Twelve grains is roughly 205 parts per million of hardness; sixteen grains is roughly 274. Those figures describe the fill water before a single gallon evaporates. If you are not sure which zone serves your home, the report includes a map and a hardness table, and Mesa Water Quality Services answers questions at 480-644-6461.

Pool service in Mesa: what owners need most

Weekly pool cleaning and maintenance is the steady work: brushing, skimming, baskets, filter checks and keeping chlorine, pH and stabilizer in range through a long summer. In a zone near 16 grains, scale on the waterline arrives faster, which is where pool tile cleaning comes in. Hard water also leaves deposits inside heaters and on salt cell plates, so people searching for pool equipment repair in Mesa, AZ, usually land on pool equipment repair or pool heater repair. Old, rough plaster is a pool resurfacing question, and Mesa has a specific rule about the wastewater from that job, covered below.

Draining a pool the way Mesa asks

Mesa's environmental team publishes step by step guidance for draining or backwashing a pool or spa. The short version: the sewer cleanout on your property is the place for it, and storm drains are not.

Use the sewer cleanout

No notification or permit is needed to drain to the sanitary sewer cleanout on your own lot. If there are two, the city says to use the one closest to the home. Mesa then treats that water and reuses it for landscape irrigation or groundwater recharge.

Go slow and watch inside

The city lists 12 gallons per minute as the maximum recommended rate, and asks that the water be close to neutral pH first. A pump that is too strong can push water back into the yard or house, so check the shower and tub drains after it starts and shut it off if water backs up. Keep sand, soil and debris out of the line.

Keep it out of the street

Mesa discourages sending pool water into the storm drain system, because storm water gets no treatment and can end up in washes, retention basins, parks and lakes. Never aim the water at a street manhole either; the city warns that can cause a sewer overflow.

Two Mesa details that catch owners out

The winter refill and your sewer fee

Mesa calculates the wastewater part of a home's bill from water use in winter. Because of that, the city notes that filling a pool between December and March can raise your sewer fee, while filling between April and November does not. If a pool company recommends draining and refilling to bring down calcium, total dissolved solids (the minerals and salts that build up as water evaporates) or stabilizer, ask whether the job can be scheduled outside those winter months.

Acid washing and replastering wastewater

The city does not allow wastewater from pool repairs such as acid washing or replastering to go to the storm sewer or the sanitary sewer, and it puts the responsibility on the property owner to make sure the repair company disposes of it properly. Before a resurfacing or acid wash, ask the company exactly what happens to that water and get the answer in writing on the quote. If you are deciding between patching and a full new surface, the repair or resurface guide walks through it.

Pool water on the landscape

Mesa also allows draining onto your own yard, as long as the water stays on your property. The city suggests waiting several days after chemical treatments so chlorine can fade, draining slowly so the soil does not flood, and using the water on salt-tolerant plants, since saltwater pools carry more salt that can harm plants and soil.

Hard water, heat and a Mesa pool

Even at the city's lower zone average, a pool in the Valley concentrates minerals every time you top it off after a hot week, because the water evaporates and the calcium stays. A careful pool technician tests calcium hardness and total dissolved solids along with the daily basics, and uses the Langelier Saturation Index (LSI), a calculation that combines pH, alkalinity, calcium and water temperature, to judge whether the water is likely to leave scale or etch plaster. Hot summer water pushes that balance toward scale.

Where your zone runs harder, the margin is smaller. Expect the company you are put through to to talk about how often to test, what the tile line looks like, and when partial or full water replacement makes sense. The guide to draining a pool in Arizona explains the signs.

  • Baskets first. Clear the skimmer and pump baskets; a clogged basket can starve the pump.
  • Read the filter gauge. Note the pressure and tell the company; high pressure usually points to a dirty filter.
  • Check the schedule. Make sure the pump timer or automation did not reset after an outage.
  • Look at the pad. Note drips or puddles around the pump, filter and heater, but do not open anything electrical.
  • Breaker once. Reset a tripped pool breaker or GFCI one time only. A second trip means leave it off and call.
  • Chemical safety. Never mix pool chemicals with each other, keep them apart, dry and shaded and out of reach of children, and follow the label.

Gas smell near a pool heater? Move away from it, leave switches and the heater alone, and once you are clear of the area phone 911 or your gas utility. Keep children away from any pool that is unfenced or uncovered, and never leave a child alone near water.

Common questions

How hard is the water in Mesa for my pool?

It depends on your zone. The City of Mesa's 2025 water quality report gives an average of about 12 grains per gallon in the City Zone and 16 grains per gallon in the Eastern and Southern zones. The city says hardness across Mesa ranges from 12 to 22 grains per gallon depending on the source serving your area. One grain per gallon equals 17.1 parts per million.

Can I drain my pool into the sewer cleanout in Mesa?

Yes. Mesa says no notification or permit is needed to drain a pool to the sanitary sewer cleanout on your own property. The city gives 12 gallons per minute as the maximum recommended discharge rate, asks for water close to neutral pH, and says to watch your shower and tub drains for backups. The city discourages sending pool water to the storm drain system.

Where does acid wash water go in Mesa?

Not into either sewer. The City of Mesa says wastewater from pool repairs such as acid washing or replastering is not allowed in the storm sewer or the sanitary sewer, and the property owner must make sure the repair company handles it properly. Ask about disposal before the job starts.

Does refilling my pool in winter raise my Mesa sewer bill?

It can. Mesa bases the wastewater charge on winter water use, so the city notes that filling a pool between December and March can affect your sewer fee. Filling between April and November has no effect on that charge.
